summary: Gives an algorithmic description of how an RSVP implementation processes messages. It is meant to clarify the version 1 specification in RFC 2205 and help implementers build programs that behave the same way. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: It is the step-by-step recipe a computer follows each time an RSVP message arrives, so every cook makes the same dish.

subtitle: The algorithmic rules that RSVP routers follow to process reservation messages.

tldr.problem: RSVP routers need to process reservation messages consistently, but the version 1 spec was vague about the exact steps involved. This meant different implementations could behave differently.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides detailed algorithms for how RSVP routers handle each type of message (PATH, RESV, PTEAR, PERR, RERR, and others) and manage the state blocks (PSB, RSB, TCSB, BSB) that track path and reservation information.
tldr.outcome: Implementers can now write RSVP software that behaves consistently with other implementations, improving interoperability and network reliability.

facts.label: Message types
facts.value: PATH, PTEAR, PERR, RESV, RTEAR, RERR, RACK

today: RFC 2209 remains an informational companion to the RSVP specification (RFC 2205). While RSVP itself is not widely deployed in the modern Internet, this memo provides the detailed algorithms that any implementation must follow.

sections.title: What This RFC Does
sections.content:
RFC 2209 provides the detailed algorithms that RSVP routers and hosts must follow to process reservation messages. While RFC 2205 specifies the RSVP protocol itself, it leaves many implementation details to the reader. This memo fills in those gaps by describing, in algorithmic form, how to process each message type and manage the state that tracks sender and reservation information.

The RFC is intended to help implementers write RSVP software that behaves consistently with other implementations, thereby improving interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: This is like the detailed recipe for how a computer should handle messages about reserving network bandwidth.

sections.title: State Blocks and Data Structures
sections.content:
RSVP routers maintain four main data structures to track state. A Path State Block (PSB) stores information about a sender and its path through the network, created when the router receives a PATH message from a sender. A Reservation State Block (RSB) stores information about a reservation request that arrived in a RESV message, including which senders to reserve bandwidth for and what quality of service to provide. A Traffic Control State Block (TCSB) holds the information that has been handed to the local traffic control system for each outgoing interface. A Blockade State Block (BSB) stores information about admission control failures to prevent reservation storms.

Each block contains specific fields: a PSB includes the session, sender, sender traffic specification, the previous hop IP address, and routing information. An RSB includes the session, next hop, filter specifications (which senders to reserve for), style, and flowspec (quality of service). A TCSB includes the session, interface, merged flowspec, and handles to the traffic control system.
sections.plainLanguage: A router keeps notes about each sender (PSB), each group of reservations (RSB), each outgoing link it is using (TCSB), and each time it had to say no (BSB).

sections.title: Processing Messages
sections.content:
When any message arrives, the router first checks the version and checksum. If the message is PATH, PTEAR, or RACK addressed to this router, it processes it; otherwise it forwards the message. The router parses all objects in the message and verifies the INTEGRITY object if present.

PATH messages carry information from a sender. The router searches for a matching PSB and either updates it or creates a new one. If the PSB is new or changed, the router triggers refreshes of both PATH and RESV messages and upcalls to local applications. RESV messages carry reservation requests. The router checks that path state exists, verifies the style is compatible with existing reservations, and then processes each flow descriptor independently or as a group depending on the style (FF, SE, or WF). It searches for matching senders, updates or creates an RSB, and triggers traffic control updates.

PTEAR messages tear down path state: the router deletes matching PSBs and associated RSBs, then forwards the PTEAR downstream. RTEAR messages tear down reservation state: the router deletes matching RSBs and may forward RTEAR upstream. PERR messages report path errors: the router forwards them toward the previous hop or upcalls to the application if the router is the sender. RERR messages report reservation errors: the router may create blockade state and forward the error toward the application.
sections.plainLanguage: PATH tells the router about a sender, RESV asks for bandwidth reserved for senders, PTEAR removes a sender, RTEAR removes a reservation, and PERR and RERR are messages saying something went wrong.

sections.title: Updating Traffic Control
sections.content:
The UPDATE TRAFFIC CONTROL sequence is invoked when path or reservation state changes, to keep the network interface in sync with what has been reserved. The router computes the effective flowspec by taking the least-upper-bound (LUB) of all matching reservation flowspecs. It searches for a matching TCSB (traffic control state block) for the interface and either creates a new one, deletes an old one, or modifies an existing one.

For a new TCSB, the router calls the traffic control system with TC_AddFlowspec to create the reservation. For an existing TCSB, if the flowspec or filter specs have changed, the router calls TC_ModFlowspec to modify the reservation or TC_DelFlowspec to delete it. The router also calls TC_AddFilter and TC_DelFilter for each filter specification.

If a RESV_CONFIRM object is present, the router either forwards it to the previous hop (via a RACK message) or moves it into the TCSB to be forwarded with the next RESV refresh, depending on whether this reservation is the largest.
sections.plainLanguage: The router tells the network interface what bandwidth to reserve and what packets to forward, and updates it when the reservations change.

sections.title: Sending Refreshes
sections.content:
RSVP state must be periodically refreshed to survive router reboots and message loss. The PATH REFRESH sequence sends a PATH message downstream to refresh path state. The router inserts a TIME_VALUES object, computes the TTL by decrementing the received TTL, creates a sender descriptor containing the SENDER_TEMPLATE, SENDER_TSPEC, and POLICY_DATA objects, and sends a copy to each outgoing interface. Before sending each copy, the router updates the ADSPEC object by calling the traffic control system and inserts the interface address and LIH into the PHOP object.

The RESV REFRESH sequence sends a RESV message upstream toward each previous hop. The router creates a message containing INTEGRITY, SESSION, RSVP_HOP, and TIME_VALUES objects, determines the style from the first matching RSB, and then for each matching PSB, selects all matching TCSB's and merges the flowspecs appropriately depending on the style (FF merges distinctly, WF and SE merge shared flowspecs). It then packs the merged flow descriptor into the message and sends to the previous hop.
sections.plainLanguage: The router sends out messages saying 'I still remember this sender' and 'I still have this reservation' so that the network does not forget about them.
